source_refs.note: Exercise 14.1, Question 11: book page 267 (PDF 272); answer key PDF 311 (book page 306).

blocks.prompt: 11 (i) Find the direction cosines for the given vector: \(\underline{u} = -6\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Direction cosines are the components of the unit vector: each component divided by the length.
Plan: find the length, divide, check that the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = -6\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\).
To find: \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(\cos\alpha = x/r\), \(\cos\beta = y/r\), \(\cos\gamma = z/r\), where \(r\) is the length.

Find the magnitude
\[r = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{49} = 7\]
Why: Magnitude formula.

Divide each component by \(7\)
\[\cos\alpha = -\dfrac{6}{7}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{3}{7}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{2}{7}\]
Why: Direction cosine = component / length.

blocks.prompt: 11 (ii) Find the direction cosines for the given vector: \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Direction cosines are the components of the unit vector: each component divided by the length.
Plan: find the length, divide, check that the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\).
To find: \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(\cos\alpha = x/r\), \(\cos\beta = y/r\), \(\cos\gamma = z/r\), where \(r\) is the length.

Find the magnitude
\[r = \sqrt{16 + 4 + 25} = \sqrt{45}\]
\[= 3\sqrt{5}\]
Why: Magnitude formula.

Divide each component by \(3\sqrt{5}\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{15}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{-5}{3\sqrt{5}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\]
Why: Direction cosine = component / length.

blocks.prompt: 11 (iii) Find the direction cosines for the given vector: \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\), where \(P(9, 3, 13)\) and \(Q(11, 6, 19)\).
blocks.explanation:
Direction cosines are the components of the unit vector: each component divided by the length.
Plan: find the vector first, then find the length, divide, check that the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\), where \(P(9, 3, 13)\) and \(Q(11, 6, 19)\).
To find: \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(\cos\alpha = x/r\), \(\cos\beta = y/r\), \(\cos\gamma = z/r\), where \(r\) is the length.

Find the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\)
\[\overrightarrow{PQ} = (11 - 9)\underline{i} + (6 - 3)\underline{j}\]
\[\quad + (19 - 13)\underline{k}\]
\[= 2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\]
Why: End point \(Q\) minus start point \(P\).

Find the magnitude
\[r = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7\]
Why: Magnitude formula.

Divide each component by \(7\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{2}{7}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{3}{7}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{6}{7}\]
Why: Direction cosine = component / length.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (PDF 311) gives answers only for 11 (i) and (ii); the answer for 11 (iii) is missing. For \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\) the direction cosines are \(\frac{2}{7}, \frac{3}{7}, \frac{6}{7}\).
